subject: A question about the bootstrapping procedure for modularity test

messages.author: 954265ab4506b84c
messages.subject: A question about the bootstrapping procedure for modularity test
parts:
Hi all,

I am using geomorph to explore the modular patterns of mammalian skulls using 3D landmarks (without semilandmarks). I run the function modularity.test including the bootstrapping procedure to compare the modularity of different samples. According to the permutation test, the CR values are significanlty low, so the modular hypothesis tested is accepted. However, the observed CR value is outside the confidence intervals obtained from the bootstrapping (for example, CR is 0.72 but the CI are from 0.74 to 0.85).

I thought that, while the CR can be lower than the random distribution of the permutation test (when it is significant), it should be always within the CI for the bootstrapping procedure.
Therefore, I may be doing something wrong when running the function or, maybe, I am wrong about what the boostrapping means.

Could anyone help me with this question?

Thanks in advance,

Best,

A L

parts:
A L,

 I can not speak to the details of how Dean & Michael set up this function (I only briefly looked at the guts of boot.CR() which can be accessed via geomorph:::boot.CR). Hopefully they will be able to give you some suggestions with respect to geomorph. However this is unfortunately a known issue with non-parametric bootstrap that pops up from time to time.  Often it occurs when your observed test statistic (in this case CR) is near a boundary/limit, but this does not seem to be the case for your statistic. 
Problems can also occur if you have a relatively small sample size and there is an outlier in the sample (that substantially alters the estimated test statistic, but the outlier is not found in many of the bootstrap samples). There are a couple of things to do/potential solutions to it. 

One thing you can check relatively easily is the bias in the estimator. You can extract the bootstrapped values from MyObject$CR.boot and compute the bias as something like

bias <- (1/iter)*sum(CR.boot - CR.est)

where iter = the number of bootstrap iterations (i.e length(MyObject$CR.boot)) CR.boot is the vector of bootstrapped CR values from MyObject$CR.boot and CR.est is the estimated CR value for your full sample (0.72 in your case). 


0) If your sample size is very small, you have to ask whether bootstrap CIs are even going to be meaningful. If I am correct (but I rarely am), I think with a sample size of N, you have (2N -1)!/(N!(N-1)) independent bootstraps. 

1) Based on the code in modularity.test() (i.e. the line of code CR.CI <- quantile(CR.boot, c(0.025, 0.975)), the particular type of bootstrap confidence intervals being used are the so-called "percentile" intervals, the 2.5% and 97.5% intervals of all of the bootstrap samples. This is known to be susceptible to some problems, and one thing that can be used (although you would have to modify the modularity.test function yourself to do so) is the bias corrected and accelerated (BCa) confidence intervals which is available in the boot library. It can also be written yourself (and I can share some VERY ugly code I wrote along time ago I wrote to make it work, but best to use boot library if you can, it is better in every way). You can access the bootstraps from your output object from modularity.test  with MyObject$CR.boot, I think (not 100% sure). However, this sometimes does not fix the problem. In which case using the bootstrap-t interval is often advocated which can be more complicated (as you will likely have to bootstrap each bootstrapped sample). 

2) The second solution that might (?) work is a transformation of the CR statistic. As I understand it, it is only bound at zero, and can take on positive values, so I don't think this will be likely to work, but may be worth a try. Maybe a Fisher's transformation or something for this. I have not really thought carefully about the properties of the statistic, and Dean Adams would be in a far better position to address this. 

Cheers
Ian

Folks,

 

Ian’s comments are exactly correct. A known pathology with the bootstrap is that occasionally the observed test value falls outside the boostrap CI range. It is uncommon, but can happen.  Ian pointed out two common reasons for this: 1) small sample sizes, 2) the observed test statistic being near its theoretical limit.  To this list I will add a third which might be the case here:  The test statistic being at its empirical limit for a particular dataset.

 

What I mean is the following. Say you have a test measure (e.g., CR) whose observed value for the data is very low. Then you find that across many, many permutations of the data, one never finds a CR value as low as the observed. Typically we think of this in terms of significance testing via permutation, but it also tells us something else: that our observed value is at the lower limit for this empirical dataset.  From this it follows that if random permutations of one block of variables relative to the other can never produce a test statistic as extreme as our observed, bootstrapping the data may not either. This could lead to the observed test value being outside the range of the bootstrap CI.

 

I suggest this as a corollary to the better-known ‘near the theoretical limit’ of the test measure. This was derived from parametric hypothesis testing theory, but the analogous reason from permutation theory should hold also.

 

Best,

 

Dean

parts:
A L,

A possibility exists that the observed CR, which is not rotationally invariant, could exist outside the bootstrapped range because of the rotation correction steps used to estimate CR in each iteration.  To be precise, CR is not a single value but a range of values for Procrustes residuals (coordinates), because rotating the orientation of the configurations will change the CR estimated, even if the configurations are unchanged.  In other words, if we make a series from 0 degrees to 360 degrees in really small increments (which we do in the function), and rotate the data space by these increments, CR is something like a sine wave - regular but not invariant.  We take the mean of this wave as the CR value (so that arbitrary rotation does not influence results).  With bootstrapped iterations, the wave can change each time, so it is possible to have an observed value outside of the bootstrapped range.

Rather, if you take the mean of the bootstrapped values - something I would recommend if doing this for confidence intervals, as by definition, that is the way it should be done - then the value has to be within the interval.  Don’t confuse the observed CR value with the central expectation from bootstrap resampling.  In fact, what you might learn is that your sample could be biased by an outlier (not sure, just a possibility).

The observed CR statistic is compared to random ones from a randomization test.  This is a hypothesis test.  The CI is more concerned with the precision of the estimate.  The mean of the bootstraps should be used here, not the observed CR.  It is nice if these values are similar, but that does not mean they should necessarily be.

Hope that helps!
Mike

AL,

 To expand a bit on the point of the small sample sizes that Dean made, a couple of points. 

First, as we mentioned earlier even if you have large enough sample sizes where a non-parametric bootstrap would be in principle reasonable, a small number of outliers (more on this below) could potentially cause the issue we mentioned. 

One thing to consider for something like the CR statistic is that it depends on the estimated covariance matrix. Without getting too into the weeds it is worth recognizing that unlike the "mean"  estimating variances and covariances well can require lots more data. In other words the sample sizes you might need to say that two means are different from one another (and in particular to have reasonable estimate the standard errors of each mean) are much less than for comparison among (co)variances. Depending on how you go about doing your estimation (and constraints you are willing to impose), this can get much worse for high dimensional phenotypes (like shape). So what seems like a perfectly reasonable sample size for estimating mean differences, may not be for covariances etc... 

Not sure if it will help, but I have some old screencasts up on youtube on bootstrapping methods (among other things, https://youtu.be/TP6r5CTd9yM). This one on Maximum likelihood estimation (https://youtu.be/wPtHpEp-jRo) may (?) have some discussion on some of these issues on estimation and variability in "means" VS variances. I can't remember if this went into these screencasts or not. These are just the R coding tutorials (the lectures were not captured). Probably lots of other tools out there that are way better though.

For outlier detection, at least in my experience, it is relatively easy to find outliers that are going to influence mean shape (and your estimates of means) via visual examination of PCs like you did, and also from outliers with respect to procrustes distance (from the overall sample, or within a group). These outliers will often influence properties of higher moments (like variances and covariances). However you may also have observations whose effects are spread out in hard to identify ways across many dimensions, but don't seem to be too extreme in any PCs for instance. 

In addition to the bias and estimates you provided, could you provide the standard deviation among bootstrap replicates (i.e. sd(MyObject$CR.boot))? This is one of the boostrap estimates of the standard error of your test statistic and It is useful to compare the magnitude of this to the bias.

Also what Dean said!

Good luck.

Ian

Folks,

 

Ian’s comments are exactly correct. A known pathology with the bootstrap is that occasionally the observed test value falls outside the boostrap CI range. It is uncommon, but can happen.  Ian pointed out two common reasons for this: 1) small sample sizes, 2) the observed test statistic being near its theoretical limit.  To this list I will add a third which might be the case here:  The test statistic being at its empirical limit for a particular dataset.

 

What I mean is the following. Say you have a test measure (e.g., CR) whose observed value for the data is very low. Then you find that across many, many permutations of the data, one never finds a CR value as low as the observed. Typically we think of this in terms of significance testing via permutation, but it also tells us something else: that our observed value is at the lower limit for this empirical dataset.  From this it follows that if random permutations of one block of variables relative to the other can never produce a test statistic as extreme as our observed, bootstrapping the data may not either. This could lead to the observed test value being outside the range of the bootstrap CI.

 

I suggest this as a corollary to the better-known ‘near the theoretical limit’ of the test measure. This was derived from parametric hypothesis testing theory, but the analogous reason from permutation theory should hold also.

 

Best,

 

Dean

A L,

 

 I can not speak to the details of how Dean & Michael set up this function (I only briefly looked at the guts of boot.CR() which can be accessed via geomorph:::boot.CR). Hopefully they will be able to give you some suggestions with respect to geomorph. However this is unfortunately a known issue with non-parametric bootstrap that pops up from time to time.  Often it occurs when your observed test statistic (in this case CR) is near a boundary/limit, but this does not seem to be the case for your statistic. 

Problems can also occur if you have a relatively small sample size and there is an outlier in the sample (that substantially alters the estimated test statistic, but the outlier is not found in many of the bootstrap samples). There are a couple of things to do/potential solutions to it. 


One thing you can check relatively easily is the bias in the estimator. You can extract the bootstrapped values from MyObject$CR.boot and compute the bias as something like

 

bias <- (1/iter)*sum(CR.boot - CR.est)

 

where iter = the number of bootstrap iterations (i.e length(MyObject$CR.boot)) CR.boot is the vector of bootstrapped CR values from MyObject$CR.boot and CR.est is the estimated CR value for your full sample (0.72 in your case). 

 

 

0) If your sample size is very small, you have to ask whether bootstrap CIs are even going to be meaningful. If I am correct (but I rarely am), I think with a sample size of N, you have (2N -1)!/(N!(N-1)) independent bootstraps. 

 

1) Based on the code in modularity.test() (i.e. the line of code CR.CI <- quantile(CR.boot, c(0.025, 0.975)), the particular type of bootstrap confidence intervals being used are the so-called "percentile" intervals, the 2.5% and 97.5% intervals of all of the bootstrap samples. This is known to be susceptible to some problems, and one thing that can be used (although you would have to modify the modularity.test function yourself to do so) is the bias corrected and accelerated (BCa) confidence intervals which is available in the boot library. It can also be written yourself (and I can share some VERY ugly code I wrote along time ago I wrote to make it work, but best to use boot library if you can, it is better in every way). You can access the bootstraps from your output object from modularity.test  with MyObject$CR.boot, I think (not 100% sure). However, this sometimes does not fix the problem. In which case using the bootstrap-t interval is often advocated which can be more complicated (as you will likely have to bootstrap each bootstrapped sample). 

 

2) The second solution that might (?) work is a transformation of the CR statistic. As I understand it, it is only bound at zero, and can take on positive values, so I don't think this will be likely to work, but may be worth a try. Maybe a Fisher's transformation or something for this. I have not really thought carefully about the properties of the statistic, and Dean Adams would be in a far better position to address this. 

 

Cheers

Ian
